claims.text: The target material class includes Ta-containing refractory high-entropy alloys.
TaNbHfZr and TaMoW are BCC solids at 0 K under the contemplated conditions.
A single-step LCP perturbation using an MTP can bypass full phase-space thermodynamic integration.
A system containing at least 500 atoms is sufficient to capture local chemical disorder in the target alloys.
Transient liquid-like clusters form within the BCC lattice and act as nucleation seeds.
The accuracy of the free-energy landscape is dictated by the MTP's representation of element-specific local coordination environments and bond lengths.
Training an MTP on high-temperature liquid data produces a smooth and accurate liquid-phase potential-energy surface.
Standard EAM potentials fail to represent the complex liquid structure of multicomponent refractory alloys.
The asserted EAM failure arises from reliance on pair correlations.
The solid-liquid free-energy difference is dominated by local structural rearrangements rather than long-range collective modes.
Restricting the perturbation calculation to a localized cluster avoids the whole-system scaling attributed to thermodynamic integration.
LCP-MTP will predict the true melting temperature within 50 K.
LCP-MTP will reduce computational cost by two orders of magnitude relative to standard TOR-TILD.
The computed solid-liquid free-energy difference will vary smoothly and monotonically with temperature.
Hysteresis artifacts are common in standard perturbation methods.
Standard TOR-TILD requires extensive sampling of the entire phase space, causing prohibitively high computational cost.
The proposed method is applicable to refractory BCC HEAs with atomic-size mismatch greater than 5% and high mixing entropy.
Strong directional bonding or extreme chemical segregation can invalidate the local-cluster approximation when those environments are absent from the training set.
Unrepresented electronic effects or solid-liquid interfacial anharmonicity can systematically bias the predicted melting point.

If poisoned and clean training sets yield statistically indistinguishable melting temperatures, the apparent result is an artifact of the perturbation scheme rather than evidence of potential accuracy.
